events.title: The birth of St. Catherine of Siena
events.shortBlurb: The Dominican mystic who would counsel popes and help return the papacy to Rome was born, by tradition, on the feast of the Annunciation…
body: Born at Siena on 25 March 1347, the feast of the Annunciation, Catherine was the youngest but one of the many children of the dyer Giacomo di Benincasa and his wife Lapa. At seven she vowed her virginity to Christ; at sixteen she took the habit of the Dominican tertiaries, passing three years in a little room of her father's house in prayer and austerity.

Emerging to nurse the sick and serve the poor, she gathered disciples and dictated letters — nearly four hundred survive — to popes and ordinary souls. At Pisa in 1375 she received the stigmata, which at her prayer remained invisible; in 1376 she went to Gregory XI at Avignon, urging him to reform the Church and return to Rome, which he did on 17 January 1377.

In the Great Schism she labored for Urban VI; she dictated her Dialogue in 1378 and, at his summons, went to Rome, where she wore out her strength for the Church's unity, dying there on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. Pius II, a Sienese, canonized her in 1461; Paul VI made her a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and John Paul II a co-patron of Europe in 1999.

events.title: The consecration of the Florence Cathedral
events.shortBlurb: Pope Eugene IV consecrated Santa Maria del Fiore as Brunelleschi's great dome, the largest since antiquity, was completed…
body: On 25 March 1436, the feast of the Annunciation and the first day of the Florentine year, Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence. The church, begun in 1296 to the design of Arnolfo di Cambio on the site of old Santa Reparata, had waited more than a century for its crowning work.

That work was the vast octagonal dome of Filippo Brunelleschi, raised between 1420 and 1436 after he won the commission in a public competition of 1418. Built of brick in a double shell without wooden centering, it spans some forty-four metres and remains the largest masonry dome ever constructed.

For the consecration the composer Guillaume Dufay wrote the motet 'Nuper rosarum flores', whose structure has often been said to mirror the proportions of the church. The day joined faith, civic pride, and the new art of the Renaissance in a single act of dedication.
